figures.caption: Figure 1 : Workflow adopted in this study for the comparative analysis of WIP and CUP cathodes. A cathode disc, prepared by either warm isostatic or conventional uniaxial pressing, was then centred on one side of the LPSCl pellet and pressed under the same load to ensure intimate interfacial contact. The counter electrode was prepared by positioning a lithium-metal disc at the center of a 9 mm diameter indium-foil disc and applying gentle manual pressure to establish a Li-In alloy contact. The resulting Li–In counter electrode was designed to provide a sufficiently large lithium reservoir and a relatively stable electrochemical potential, such that the measured cell response is predominantly governed by the composite cathode under investigation. figures.caption: Figure 2: Schematic of the DEM-based modeling workflow for the slurry-based manufacturing and pressing of the composite cathode. The dried electrode serves as the common initial structure for the CUP and WIP routes, followed by post-pressing recovery. The blue particles represent AM, the white particles SE, and the red particles CBD. 2.4.1 Dried and pressed composite cathode microstructures As illustrated in Figure 2, CUP and WIP were simulated from the same dried cathode microstructure generated from an identical slurry formulation. The DEM models were formulated as through-thickness internal representative volume element (RVE) representations of the corresponding experimental processing routes. figures.caption: Figure 4 : Cross-sectional microstructural characterization of the unpressed, CUP, and WIP composite cathodes. a) Cross-sectional SEM micrographs showing the reduction in cathode thickness. b) Corresponding EDS elemental maps showing the spatial distributions of C, O, Ni, Co, Mn, and Al within the composite cathodes. The WIP cathode exhibits a more compact and homogeneous particle arrangement than the CUP and unpressed cathodes.

figures.caption: Figure 5 : XCT results. (a) Exemplary XCT cross sections of CUP and WIP composite cathodes. The corresponding image above represents a vertical cross section and the lower an in-plane cross section. (b) 3D rendering of the segmented active material particles. (c) Perpendicular to the cathode plane/CC summed intensity. (d) In-plane summed intensity, displaying a 2D projection of the 3D binary image stack. (e) 2D distribution of the distances between the AM particles closest to the current collector and the closest to the surface particle on the opposite side in thickness direction of the cathode. If no particles are within one column from the current collector to the surface, the value is equal zero. (f) Histogram of the distance distribution of Figure 2e. Only the higher values correspond to the thickness of the cathode.
